deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the theory of the instrumental errors of a meridian transit instrument, as used in practical astronomy, for example at the Göttingen observatory. It has nothing to do with the hypergeometric and Legendre material on the neighbouring page.

Figure: a spherical triangle drawn inside a circle, presumably the sphere or horizon.
- One side is marked δ (declination) and another 90°+c.
- The angles are marked a and α (a second small mark at the lower vertex is hard to read).
- My interpretation: the vertices are the pole, the end of the instrument's rotation axis and the star. The star lies at 90°+c from the axis end, where c is the collimation error. The axis end is displaced from its ideal position by the inclination i and the azimuth error a.

Line 1: c/cosδ + i(cosφ cosδ + sinφ sinδ) + a(sinφ cosδ − cosφ sinδ).
- Here φ is the geographic latitude.
- Read with an implicit overall factor 1/cosδ on the last two terms (my supplement), this is Tobias Mayer's formula for the correction to the observed transit time: τ = [c + i cos(φ−δ) + a sin(φ−δ)]/cosδ.
- The bracket after i is cos(φ−δ); the bracket after a is sin(φ−δ).

Line 2: i cosφ + a sinφ. This is Bessel's constant m.

Line 3: dividing out by cosδ gives
c/cosδ + i cosφ + a sinφ + (i sinφ − a cosφ) tgδ.
- This is Bessel's form τ = m + n tanδ + c secδ, with m = i cosφ + a sinφ and n = i sinφ − a cosφ.
- Explicitly: i cos(φ−δ)/cosδ = i cosφ + i sinφ tanδ, and a sin(φ−δ)/cosδ = a sinφ − a cosφ tanδ.

Line 4: a struck-out start ("c + i …") and an isolated "sinδ" with an overbar, apparently a denominator.

Lines 5–8: the polar distance p = 90°−δ is introduced, so secδ = 1/sin p and tanδ = cot p.
- The c and n part of the correction becomes c/sin p + n cos p/sin p.
- Substitute cos p = cos²(p/2) − sin²(p/2) and 1 = cos²(p/2) + sin²(p/2) (both written on the page).
- Use sin p = 2 sin(p/2) cos(p/2) (my supplement).
- Result: (c + n cos p)/sin p = ((c+n)/2) cot(p/2) + ((c−n)/2) tan(p/2).
- Purpose: for stars near the pole (small p) the correction is dominated by (c+n)/2 · cot(p/2). Observing such stars therefore separates the combinations c+n and c−n, which is useful for determining collimation and azimuth from circumpolar stars, e.g. upper and lower culminations.
errors: Line 1 omits the overall division by cosδ of the i- and a-terms, and parentheses around the a-bracket. This is notational shorthand; line 3 shows the intended quantity was divided by cosδ.
No mathematical errors: the expansion into Bessel's m, n, c form and the half-angle rewriting are both correct.

results.what: Correction of transit time for collimation c, inclination i and azimuth a: [c + i cos(φ−δ) + a sin(φ−δ)]/cosδ
Rewriting as m + n tanδ + c secδ with m = i cosφ + a sinφ, n = i sinφ − a cosφ
results.modern_name: Bessel's formula for the transit instrument

results.what: (c + n cos p)/sin p = (c+n)/2 cot(p/2) + (c−n)/2 tan(p/2) in terms of polar distance p
results.modern_name: half-angle decomposition of the collimation/azimuth terms (textbook practical astronomy)

deep.surprise_reason: Standard textbook reduction of transit-instrument errors (Mayer and Bessel forms) with an elementary half-angle identity. It is routine for a Göttingen student exposed to observatory practice and has no mathematical novelty.

checkable.sympy: simplify((c + i*cos(phi-delta) + a*sin(phi-delta))/cos(delta) - (c/cos(delta) + i*cos(phi) + a*sin(phi) + (i*sin(phi) - a*cos(phi))*tan(delta)))
checkable.asserts: Mayer form equals Bessel form m + n tanδ + c secδ (result 0)
half-angle decomposition of the c and n terms (result 0)

transcription_corrections: Line 2 'ȯ cosφ + a sinφ' should read 'i cosφ + a sinφ' (Bessel's m).
Line 1: the a-term is a(sinφ cosδ − cosφ sinδ), with the bracket closing after sinδ. The closing parenthesis visible after 'sinδ)' belongs to the i-term.
Line 3: the blotted operator in '(i sinφ • a cosφ)' must be a minus sign: (i sinφ − a cosφ) tgδ.
Figure: the side labels are δ and 90°+c; the angle labels are α near the upper right vertex and a at the lower vertex (with an additional unclear mark, possibly i).
